description: Thin variant of ThreePushPattern: at least minLegs alternating pivots where BOTH sides diverge — each swing high above the swing high two pivots back and each swing low below the swing low two pivots back.

complexity.reason: same pivot machinery as ThreePushPattern, applied to both sides across five or more pivots

merge_notes: Kept as a thin variant rather than a parameterization because the two-sided divergence test is not expressible as ThreePushPattern(shapeMode=2), which only looks at one side's pushes. V06-01's five-leg two-sided form is the definition; VP1-17 is the same with three pushes; V24-19's one-sided form (each push exceeds the prior by >= 4 ticks) is ThreePushPattern with minPushExtensionTicks = 4 and is recorded as that parameterization, not a separate detector. V06-06 ('a failed breakout grows it to seven then nine legs') is the same rule with minLegs as a lower bound, exactly as its own note concedes. The reversal entry off the pattern is ThreePushReversalEntry; the target is SwingPivotTarget.

description: Three pushes in which each new extreme beats the prior one by only a tick or two, then price closes beyond the LAST push's extreme — a wedge that fails to reverse and instead breaks out with the pushes.
pseudocode: isThreePushPattern[0] with maxPushExtensionTicks = 2 && close[0] > swingHigh(1, swingStrength)

complexity.reason: pivot detection plus a per-push extension cap in ticks

merge_notes: Stray, absorbed. Behaviourally the opposite trade to ThreePushSwingBreakoutEntry (with the pushes, not against them), so kept separate despite sharing the primitive. The source's 3-to-20-bar pullback between the marginal breakouts is exactly what a confirmed pivot at swingStrength 2 already enforces, so it is not carried as a second parameter.

description: Named Brooks setup: a three-push pattern whose MIDDLE push is the most extreme and whose two outer pushes are roughly equal — a head-and-shoulders top (mirrored for a bottom).
pseudocode:
ls = swingHigh(3, s); head = swingHigh(2, s); rs = swingHigh(1, s);
isHeadAndShouldersTop = head > ls && head > rs && absValue(ls - rs) <= shoulderSymmetryTicks * tick

complexity.reason: ThreePushPattern's pivots with the ordering test changed from monotone to peaked, plus a symmetry tolerance

merge_notes: Kept as a named composite (Brooks calls it a wedge whose third push fails to surpass the second) because Brian would want it tested as the book states it. It is NOT ThreePushPattern at a parameter: the monotone 'each push beyond the last' test is replaced by a peaked one, so different bars. R12-04's head-and-shoulders CONTINUATION variant is the same shape plus a double top/bottom around the right shoulder; the double-top half is swing_structure's rule, AND-ed as its own pane. The neckline is not in this rule — see HeadAndShouldersNecklineBreakout.

description: The literal head-and-shoulders entry: price closes beyond the neckline, the line through the two pullback extremes between the shoulders and the head.
pseudocode:
necklinePrice = lineValue(swingLow(3, s), swingLow(2, s), currentBarIndex);
isHeadAndShouldersTop[0] && close[0] < necklinePrice - entryTick * tick

complexity.reason: inherits the pattern's pivots and adds a two-point line projected to the current bar

merge_notes: Kept because it is the textbook entry Brooks is arguing AGAINST ('a breakout below the neckline in a bull market will usually fail'), which makes it worth testing as stated — and testable negated, which is the trade he recommends.

description: The high and low made in the premarket/overnight window are held as levels through the day session; the bar tests one of them within a tick tolerance. Brooks treats the premarket extremes as targets that usually get tested once the day session opens.
pseudocode:
if (ctx.Time(0) > premarketStart && ctx.Time(0) <= premarketEnd) { pmHigh = MaxList(pmHigh, high[0]); pmLow = MinList(pmLow, low[0]) }  /* reset at the session date change */
ctx.Time(0) > premarketEnd && high[0] >= pmHigh - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: segments each session's bars into a premarket window by clock time, accumulates an extreme over just that window, and holds it for the rest of the session

merge_notes: Only one candidate, and the only rule in the bucket that needs a SECOND session window (premarket) beside the day session; it therefore rides on whatever session model the design decision settles. Requires the data feed to include Globex/overnight bars - on a regular-session-only series the rule can never fire. Same shape as PriorSessionLevelTest but the level comes from a within-day window rather than the previous session, so they are kept apart.

description: The prior session closed strong - its close was near the high of its final closingWindowBars bars - which biases the next session bullish. A flag computed at one session's end and consulted through the next.
pseudocode:
at the last bar of a session: closedStrong = close[0] >= highest(high, closingWindowBars) - toleranceTicks * tickSize;
during the next session: return closedStrong

complexity.reason: needs session-END detection (the bar before a date change is only knowable one bar late, or via a session-close clock time) and state carried across the boundary

catalog_match.note: same 'where did it close in the range' idea, but over the session's closing window and carried into the next session

merge_notes: Brooks's point is about the daily bar's shape: a 5-minute rally into the close makes the daily bar a bull trend bar and biases the next bar. Note the mechanization trap: the last bar of a session is only identifiable one bar late (when Date changes) unless a session-close clock time is an input; the clock-time form is the cheaper one and matches the corpus's TimeWindow habit. closingWindowMinutes 45 in the book = 9 five-minute bars.

description: After price briefly trades beyond a recent swing extreme against the trade direction but immediately closes back in the trend direction, enter (or re-enter) on a stop one tick beyond the prior bar's extreme.
pseudocode: stopRunOccurred = low[1] < recentSwingExtreme && close[1] > recentSwingExtreme; enterLongNextOpen = stopRunOccurred && high[0] >= high[1] + entryTick

complexity.reason: needs a tracked recent swing-extreme/stop-cluster level and a breach-then-reclaim detector before the ordinary stop-entry mechanization

merge_notes: Source frames this as 'add to or re-enter' a swing position (multi-unit language), but the mechanism itself -- a breach-and-reclaim of a recent level, entered on a stop -- does not require holding multiple units. Reduces to a single-position Entry (a stop-run continuation entry); mechanized that way, dropping the 'add to an already-open position' framing.
